analysis.one_liner: Blocks the EPA and Army Corps from using new guidance to expand which waters the Clean Water Act protects.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 28 Senate Republicans, was referred to the Environment and Public Works Committee and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: After two Supreme Court rulings left unclear exactly which streams, wetlands, and small waterways count as "waters of the United States" under the Clean Water Act, the EPA and Army Corps proposed guidance to define the scope. This bill would bar the agencies from finalizing that guidance or anything like it, and would let courts throw out any future rule built on it. In practice, it would lock in the narrower, post-2006 reading of which waters federal pollution protections cover.
analysis.who_benefits: Landowners and businesses that discharge into or build on streams, wetlands, and drainage ditches: homebuilders, farm operations, mining and energy companies. They would avoid the permitting requirements, costs, and potential legal liability that come with federal jurisdiction over more waters, and gain certainty that any rule resembling the guidance could be struck down in court.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Developers, farm operations, mining and energy firms

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits the Army Secretary and EPA Administrator from finalizing the 2011 draft guidance on identifying waters protected by the Clean Water Act, or using it or any substantially similar guidance as the basis for any decision or rulemaking [S2] [S3].
If agencies relied on the guidance or anything similar to write a rule, that rule would be vulnerable to being vacated in court, giving regulated businesses a ready-made legal defense [S3].

analysis.who_pays: People who rely on the smaller streams and wetlands that would fall outside federal pollution protections under the narrower reading, including downstream drinking water supplies. Taxpayers who use public waters for recreation would also bear any loss of protection.

drawbacks.text: Blocking the guidance would leave in place the confusion that followed two Supreme Court decisions, in which jurisdiction over small streams and wetlands turned on case-by-case fact-finding; the bill would prevent agencies from resolving it through ordinary guidance or rulemaking [S3].

The bill goes beyond stopping one document: it bars "any substantially similar guidance" and voids rules built on it, which would constrain future administrations from clarifying Clean Water Act jurisdiction at all, whatever the scientific merits [S3].

Supporters of agency action argued smaller streams and wetlands feed drinking water supplies and filter pollution, so leaving them unprotected shifts costs to downstream water users; the bill offers no alternative protection for those waters.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers real benefits to landowners and regulated businesses in the form of lower compliance costs and legal certainty. The cost is that waters currently outside a clear federal shield, small streams and wetlands, could be filled, polluted, or developed with no federal backstop, and the bill forecloses the standard administrative process for deciding where the line should be drawn. The imbalance runs toward the regulated interests.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on May 22, 2013, read twice, and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, where no further action was ever taken and the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator John Barrasso introduced the Preserve the Waters of the United States Act on May 22, 2013, joined by 27 Republican cosponsors, all from the Senate's Republican caucus [S1] [S4].
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works [S5].
No committee markup, hearing action on the bill, floor vote, or other action appears in the record after the referral; the bill died when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the EPA and Army Corps retained the ability to issue guidance and rules defining which waters are protected, and downstream communities kept the existing federal protections over streams and wetlands. The developers, farm, and extractive interests that sought a statutory bar on expanded jurisdiction did not get it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Downstream communities and the agencies' water rules

for.name: Sen. John Barrasso
for.role: Senate Republican from Wyoming; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to prohibit the EPA and Army Corps from finalizing or relying on the waters-of-the-US guidance.

against.name: Sen. Barbara Boxer
against.role: Chair, Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never brought the bill up for committee consideration, leaving it referred and unmarked-up through the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 28 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, and no Democrat signed on; the bill then died in a committee chaired by a Democrat.

industries.note: Broader federal jurisdiction over streams and wetlands triggers permitting requirements and restrictions on filling or building near covered waters; blocking the guidance spares them those costs and liabilities, while the unprotected waters are ones downstream communities rely on.

Farm groups feared the guidance would bring ditches, drainage ways, and seasonal streams under Clean Water Act permitting; the bill would prevent that outcome by statute and void any similar future rule.

industries.industry: Mining, oil and gas, and other industrial dischargers
industries.note: These industries face permitting and discharge limits where federal jurisdiction attaches; a narrower jurisdiction map reduces their compliance costs, and the bill's vacation provision would give them a standing legal argument against future rules.
